characters/agent-ben.title: Agent Ben
characters/agent-ben.content:
Agent Ben
A former L. Corp agent who now serves as a trusted advisor to the Community. Bald. Wears a white business shirt with rolled sleeves. His signature aviator shades were broken during the events of Day 07. Runs things at the Community alongside Dux, though his authority is limited — Dux considers him an advisor, not a commander.
DM Note: Ben is blind. This is not publicly known and the players do not know this. Clues in the raw data: he navigates by touch (lightly pressing on furniture for support), misses objects slid to him, does not look at items presented to him, and his folder from Koller’s visit goes unread.
History
He recognized Pug and Burr’s handguns for what they were. Kept their secret. Returned Pug’s weapon after the first warehouse mission. Cautious, measured, and clearly connected to the old world.
The Photograph
A faded photograph found in the Founder’s Apartment shows the Founder, a mechanic, and a young Ben — all three together before the apartment fell into disuse. The photograph was hidden behind a larger picture frame, taped to the back. An unknown key was also found taped to the back of the frame; the filename indicates it opens the Mechanic’s Workshop hatch.
Ben appears in the photograph as a younger man, suggesting a personal history with both the Founder and the Mechanic that predates his role at the Community.
Information Provided

Ben provides directions to the Founder’s Apartment.
Koller provides directions to the buried facility (Fallen Wing).

Day 07
Found beaten and bloodied near the Death’s Head checkpoint. His aviator sunglasses lay broken at his feet. Three scavengers had been standing over him. They fled at the sight of Pug and Burr in full armor. Ben was barely conscious — eyes glazed, pulse weak, blood dripping from his mouth. He did not know who attacked him. “Several men. Didn’t say anything.”
Pug carried him toward the Community gate. The guards refused to open the gate. Standoff ensued. During the chaos, Ben was carried through the open gate by Community guards while Burr was distracted by the electrified spike strips. His status after capture is unknown.
Relationships

Dux — Co-leader of the Community. Ben is his advisor, not his equal.
Pug — Ben returned Pug’s weapon. Trusted enough to keep their secrets.
Burr — Ben recognized Burr’s weapon and kept silent.
The Founder — Personal connection. Appears together in the photograph.
The Mechanic — Personal connection. Appears together in the photograph.
Koller — Ben provides directions to Koller’s office. Koller provides services to the Community.

characters/agent-es.title: Agent Es
characters/agent-es.content:
Agent Es
An unknown figure who goes around slaughtering the Death’s Head and wearing their gear to sow confusion and fear. His goal is the destabilization and overturning of the Death’s Head rule in the area. He wears the gear of fallen Death’s Head members, making it difficult for the syndicate to distinguish friend from foe during conflict. Players will not initially know he is an agent — he appears only as a mysterious third party in the territorial struggle.

characters/agent-jasper.title: Agent Jasper
characters/agent-jasper.content:
Agent Jasper
A man in a charcoal grey suit found in an apartment building the agents investigated. Died clutching his chest, empty handgun repeatedly clicking, unable to stop pulling the trigger even after the magazine was spent. Choked out his name but could not say more before slipping away. His body was laid on the bed, his handgun placed in his hands by Burr.
A fallen feather — former L. Corp agent, like Pug and Burr.

characters/agent-scoot.title: Agent Scoot
characters/agent-scoot.content:
Agent Scoot
A young woman who operates under the alias “Lavender.” Her true identity is Agent Scoot. She has lavender-colored hair and wears a cloth facemask with three thin white lines on either side — resembling whiskers — which she keeps pulled up to obscure her lower face. When moving through the city, she dons a raincoat with the hood drawn over her head, shrouding her face entirely.
Alias: Lavender
She uses the name “Lavender” when introduced to the agents. When asked why she hides her face, she responds: “Safer that way.” When asked for a name, she says: “Sure. Lavender works. That sounds cute.”
The name appears to be chosen on the spot — a casual alias rather than a long-standing identity. The lavender hair makes it fitting.
The Fallen Wing
Lavender was present in the Fallen Wing facility alongside the agents during Day 07. She guided them through the underground, provided intelligence on the relics, and fought the Accepted during the night. She is a capable combatant — she took on multiple Accepted members alone through three waves of night before one of them cornered her and force-attuned to the Skull Mace.
She kept the glass dagger safe throughout the ordeal, hiding it behind a bed in a burned-out room.
Intelligence Network
Lavender possesses significant knowledge about the relics, Enkephalin, and the Accepted. She:

Orchestrated blindfolded Messengers to guide the agents to specific locations
Knew about the Skull Mace and Glass Dagger before the agents did
Knew about the Enkephalin retrieved from the facility
Recognized Burr’s corporate suit from the entombed building
Understood relic attunement mechanics and matching suits
Had a card with an address where she could be found for future contact

She describes herself as wanting to “recover some of what we’ve lost” — implying the relics belonged to her or her organization originally.
Combat Capability
Lavender fought the Accepted through three waves of night in the Backstreets. She eliminated most of them before one cornered her and forced attunement to the Skull Mace. When the agents arrived, she was wounded, unarmed, and her raincoat was torn to shreds — but alive. She directed Pug and Burr in the fight against the attuned Accepted.
Post-Combat
After the fight, she:

Healed alongside Burr via Karla’s prayers
Retrieved the glass dagger from her hiding spot
Received the Enkephalin canisters from the agents
Provided 100,000 SAU as a signing bonus
Gave the agents her card with an address for future contact
Took Karla into her care

Personality

Pragmatic. She uses Messengers and aliases to maintain distance and safety.
Capable. She fights well enough to take on multiple Accepted alone.
Guarded. She hides her face and reveals little about herself.
Calm under pressure. Even when wounded and facing an attuned enemy, she directs the agents coherently.
Playful. She stifles laughter at the agents’ antics. She chose the name “Lavender” because it “sounds cute.”

Relationships

Pug — Working relationship. She provided intel and payment.
Burr — Working relationship. She found him entertaining.
Karla — Took Karla into her care after the fight.
The Accepted — Adversarial. She fought them and escaped.
The Messengers — She employed blindfolded individuals to guide the agents.

Associated Items

Raincoat (worn, hood drawn)
Cloth facemask (three thin white lines on either side)
Card with address (given to agents)

characters/backstreets-scavenger-leader.title: Backstreets Scavenger Leader
characters/backstreets-scavenger-leader.content:
Backstreets Scavenger Leader
Sometimes a Backstreets Scavenger rises above the rest and manages to gather a small following. These leaders are typically more experienced, better armed, and possess the charisma or brutality needed to keep a group together. They may claim territory, organize raids, or provide “protection” to those too weak to refuse.
Still a scavenger at heart — driven by survival and opportunity, not ideology.

characters/backstreets-scavenger.title: Backstreets Scavenger
characters/backstreets-scavenger.content:
Backstreets Scavenger
A common type found throughout the Backstreets of the City. Desperate survivors scraping by on whatever they can find, steal, or take from others. Generally armed with improvised or low-quality weapons. They organize into loose groups for protection and predation, but have no formal hierarchy or syndicate allegiance.
When they find something worth fighting for, they fight. When the odds turn, they scatter.

characters/community-founder.title: Community Founder
characters/community-founder.content:
The Founder
An unnamed individual who once lived in the Founder’s Apartment. The apartment was found in a state of disuse, its former occupants having departed or perished. The apartment contained a hidden floor lockbox, a cabinet safe, and a bedroom safe, all secured by keys found in a vase.
The Photograph
A faded photograph was found taped to the back of a picture frame in the apartment’s hallway, hidden from casual view. It depicts three people: the Founder, a mechanic, and a young Ben. All three appear in casual attire, suggesting a personal rather than professional relationship. The photograph predates the apartment’s abandonment.
An unknown key was also found taped to the back of the frame. The filename indicates it opens the Mechanic’s Workshop.
Connections

The Mechanic — Appeared alongside the Founder in the photograph. Operates a separate workshop from Koller’s. Personal connection.
Agent Ben — Appeared as a young man in the photograph alongside the Founder and the Mechanic. Provides directions to the Founder’s Apartment.
Koller — Separate from the Mechanic. Provides directions to the buried facility (Fallen Wing). Offers services to the Community.

Status
Unknown. The apartment was abandoned. The Founder’s fate is not recorded in any document found to date.
Associated Items

Picture, Founder’s Apartment — The photograph showing the Founder, the Mechanic, and young Ben
Key, Unknown — Found taped to the back of the picture frame; believed to open the Mechanic’s Workshop hatch
Key, Founder’s Apartment - Cabinet
Key, Founder’s Apartment - Closet Safe
Key, Founder’s Apartment - Hidden Floor Lockbox

characters/community-head-guard-dux.title: Community Head Guard Dux
characters/community-head-guard-dux.content:
Community Head Guard Dux
The head of the Community guard. Wears ragtag armor — a shiny grey vest, construction helmet, sportswear kneepads — and carries a crowbar. Found Pug and Burr wandering the streets after they passed through the metal barricade from the rainy district.
He is decisive and action-oriented. Disagreed with Ben’s cautious approach and chose to march against the Death’s Head anyway. Leads from the front.

characters/community-laborer-chert.title: Community Laborer Chert
characters/community-laborer-chert.content:
Community Laborer Chert
A young woman who arrived at the Community recently. Does not remember much — fell and hit her head, woke up in the Community. Joined the warehouse raid as a favor, armed with a baseball bat. Quiet, uncertain about violence, but willing to help.
She found purpose in the kitchen afterward, assisting with meal preparation. Prefers that over combat duty.

characters/community-laborer-kellestine.title: Community Laborer Kellestine
characters/community-laborer-kellestine.content:
Community Laborer Kellestine
A bald, loud, self-aggrandizing man who talks constantly about his prowess. Joined the warehouse raid alongside Pug, Burr, and Chert. Claims he was a killer back before the fall. Wears a helmet to hide his shiny bald head from snipers.
Arms himself with a tire iron. Excitable and eager to prove himself, though his actual combat experience is questionable. Has an odd charm beneath the bluster.

characters/community-mechanic.title: Community Mechanic
characters/community-mechanic.content:
The Mechanic
A person depicted in a faded photograph found in the Founder’s Apartment. The photograph shows the Founder, the Mechanic, and a young Ben together before the apartment fell into disuse. Described as “a scruffy, but nerdy looking guy.”
Role
The Mechanic was the Founder’s other closest friend, having known him far longer than Ben. He used to supply arms and armaments to the Community from his workshop. When the Founder left and left Ben “in charge,” the Mechanic continued to supply the Community for a time.
The Mechanic’s Workshop
Located in the basement of the Mechanic’s apartment, accessible via a hatch. Ben visited once but never went downstairs to the workshop. The Mechanic was “real proud of the hatch” — he and the Founder had a good laugh and boast about it together. The key found in the Founder’s Apartment (taped behind the photograph) opens this hatch.
Disappearance
After the Founder went on his journey and never came back, the Mechanic never returned to his workshop. He stayed at the Community for a good while, then went out on a job and never came back. It is assumed he went after the Founder’s trail to find him. He left Ben “in the dark” — both figuratively and literally, as Ben is blind but this is not publicly known.
Connections

The Founder — The Mechanic’s closest friend. They had known each other far longer than either had known Ben. The Mechanic was devastated by the Founder’s departure.
Agent Ben — The other person in the photograph. The Mechanic and Ben would often go to the Founder’s Apartment, the Mechanic more than Ben, as he had known the Founder far longer.
The Community — The Mechanic supplied arms and armaments to the Community from his workshop. He continued this role after the Founder left, until his own disappearance.

Locations

The Mechanic’s Apartment — East of the Community, in uncontrolled territory.
The Mechanic’s Workshop — Basement of the apartment, accessed via hatch. Opened with the key from the Founder’s Apartment photograph.
The Founder’s Apartment — West of the Community, on the other side of Death’s Head territory. Ben provided directions.

Status
Unknown. Assumed to have left after the Founder to find him. His workshop remains locked and abandoned.
Associated Items

Key, Unknown — Found in the Founder’s Apartment; opens the Mechanic’s Workshop hatch
Picture, Founder’s Apartment — The photograph showing the Mechanic alongside the Founder and young Ben

characters/death's-head-armored-biker.title: Death's Head Armored Biker
characters/death's-head-armored-biker.content:
Death’s Head Armored Biker
An elite member of the Death’s Head biker gang. Heavily armored in boots, leather pants, shoulderpads, and gloves, wearing road goggles and motorcycle helmets. Tougher and more disciplined than common thugs.
They serve as the backbone of the Death’s Head offensive and defensive operations — breaking enemy lines, protecting retreats, and engaging the most dangerous opponents.

characters/death's-head-prospect.title: Death's Head Prospect
characters/death's-head-prospect.content:
Death’s Head Prospect
A member of the Death’s Head biker gang. Low-ranking enforcers and foot soldiers. They wear leathers, white shirts, jeans, and leather vests — some with sleeves, some without. Armed with tire irons, wrenches, claw hammers, and other blunt weapons.
They control territory in the Backstreets through intimidation and force, extorting locals and muscling out rival groups. Their reach has expanded since the fall of the Wing.

characters/death's-head-warehouse-guard-.title: Death's Head Warehouse Guard Jerry
characters/death's-head-warehouse-guard-.content:
Death’s Head Warehouse Guard Jerry
A member of the Death’s Head gang stationed at the warehouse district. Encountered during the Community’s raid. Charged Pug with a pipe and was killed when a rusted knife was stabbed into his throat — the handle separated from the blade on impact, leaving the blade lodged inside him.
A minor figure, remembered only because someone called out his name as he fell.

characters/german-doctor.title: German Doctor
characters/german-doctor.content:
German Doctor
Identity
Age: Unknown. Name: Unknown. The doctor has never given a name, and neither agent has asked. He is identified only by his German accent and his profession.
Description
The doctor is a man of indeterminable age, seen wearing a once-white smock over a white dress shirt with sleeves rolled up. He wears small round spectacles, a medical mask, and mismatched latex gloves — one blue, one light red. He speaks with a thick German accent softened by years in the City’s backstreets.
He keeps a cage of white doves at the reception desk of his clinic. He speaks to them in a foreign language to calm them when they grow distressed.
Personality
Professional but eccentric, with an experimental bent. He finds genuine fascination in medical edge cases and unusual patient responses. He delivered the news of Burr’s recovery with a joke about guts that did not land. He is willing to work within a patient’s budget, adjusting treatment plans to fit available funds.
Skills
A highly skilled surgeon specializing in advanced trauma treatment. The doctor is one of the few practitioners in the backstreets capable of administering combined heliapoeisis and fibrous mechanite therapy — a dual treatment he notes had never been trialed simultaneously before Burr’s case. He can install gestator implants for severe tissue regeneration.
Connections

Backstreets Clinic — The doctor operates this clinic.
Koller — Familiar with the underground information broker.
Key, Clinic - Hospital Room — Issued to Pug for visiting Burr during recovery.

characters/koller.title: Koller
characters/koller.content:
Koller
A blind, Czech-accented Fixer operating from a workshop deep in the Backstreets. Offers medical diagnostics, augment installation, and information brokering. Speaks with a distinctive Slavic accent, frequently using the Czech word pritel (“friend”).
Personality

Jovial and eccentric. Greets people with casual warmth, uses pritel liberally. Has a dark sense of humour and does not mince words about the state of his clients (“He looks like he is dying”).
Surprisingly competent. Despite his blindness, operates computers, games, and surveillance feeds. Maintains a functioning underground workshop with medical and cybernetic equipment.
Independent. Not part of the Community but offers his services to them. Maintains his own client network and supply chains.
Business-minded. Will not work for free except for diagnostics. Has a clear augment installation policy: “bring the prosthetics, I install them.”

Physical Description
Blind. Wears an eyemask over his eyes and headphones when sleeping. Speaks with a Czech-influenced accent. Typically found in his workshop chair with a bong nearby. Prosthetic hands that he swaps out from plastic bags.
Workshop (“The Time Machine” / Koller’s Bunker)
Located deep underground, accessible via a rickety elevator that descends ominously. The workshop features:

Ceiling: Dozens (approaching a hundred) prosthetic and cybernetic arms hanging like ornaments
Workstations: Multiple workshop stations and a surgery area
Living area: Low couch, two beanbag chairs, flatscreen TV
Computer station: Half a dozen monitors, keyboards, tablets, phones connected by DIY wiring
Bedroom: A small door behind which Koller was once found eating ice cream on the toilet

Affiliation & Network

Oufi Association: Acts as a subcontractor for Oufi contracts. Handles indemnity payments (purple parcels, 100,000 SAU each per recent contract).
The Community: Offers services but is not a member. Ben provides directions to his office.
Devyat 9 (The Stray Dogs): Has dealt with them in the past. Considers them “bad for business.”
Mysterious client with white hair: Exchanges packages — Koller receives items and provides green vials in return. The client appears to be a Fixer of some seniority.

characters/pound-inmate.title: Pound Inmate
characters/pound-inmate.content:
Pound Inmate
Inmates held within the Death’s Head Pound — a repurposed school turned maximum-security prison. These are convicted criminals, captured enemies of the Death’s Head, and those awaiting processing into indentured labor. Conditions are brutal, resources are scarce, and the inmate hierarchy is enforced through violence. Most are armed with improvised weapons or bare hands.
When a disturbance occurs — an escape attempt, a riot, or an external attack — the inmates are as likely to fight the intruders as they are to seize the opportunity for freedom.

characters/stray-dog-packleader-bosco.title: Stray Dog Packleader Bosco
characters/stray-dog-packleader-bosco.content:
Stray Dog Packleader Bosco
The Pack Leader that Pug and Burr encountered operating in Death’s Head territory. Known to Maisner as “the fuck that went and croaked over in ‘yer territory.” Also goes by the alias Rex.
Status
Deceased. Killed in Pug and Burr’s territory. His death was unforeseen — no formal assault preceded it, and none of his subordinates were killed alongside him. The exact circumstances and the identity of the one who killed him remain unconfirmed.
Role in the Expedition
Bosco was not sent to District 12 because he was valuable. He was sent because he was dead weight — a problematic member the Stray Dogs wanted to shed. A lone wolf who despised management and wanted nothing more than to rampage, Bosco was the kind of Pack Leader who made his superiors desperate to find a way to dispose of him without the mess of an internal execution.
The expedition to District 12 provided that opportunity. He was chosen for the force precisely because his undesirable traits made him a liability in structured District 22 operations. In the fallen district, his violence could be directed outward rather than inward.
Personality
A lone wolf by nature. Bosco kept his packmates at arm’s length, splitting them into smaller unofficial groups to manage his territory rather than maintaining a cohesive chain of command. He had little interest in administration, logistics, or the politics of syndicate expansion. He wanted territory to fight over and enemies to break.
This made him operationally useful in bursts but structurally corrosive. A Pack Leader who does not maintain his own command structure creates a unit that cannot function without him. When he fell, his pack did not rally. It fragmented.
Legacy
Bosco’s death left approximately 50 packmates orphaned and directionless. Because he had already split them into scattered small groups, no single successor could step in to claim his command. With no chain of command, no Pack Handler response (the Handler is still assessing whether the death was a mistake or an organized attack), and no clear path back to District 22, his people have scattered:

A portion has gone feral, forming roaming bands with no leadership.
A portion has integrated into local District 12 syndicates and communities.
A portion has successfully reintegrated with other Packs.
The remainder are dead, killed in the chaos or lost to the fog.

Bosco’s death did more damage to the Stray Dogs expedition than a single Pack Leader’s loss should have. His failure to build a proper command structure ensured that the damage spread beyond his grave.
Appearances

6-9C The Stray Dog — Bosco encountered in the Death’s Head Pound, operating in their territory
15-2E Intel — Maisner confirms Bosco was a Pack Leader who died in the agents’ territory
Day 15 Summary — Summary references confirming Bosco’s role and the intel

characters/stray-dog-packleader-marco.title: Stray Dog Packleader Marco
characters/stray-dog-packleader-marco.content:
Stray Dog Packleader Marco
A Pack Leader in the Stray Dogs expeditionary force. Of the six Pack Leaders sent to District 12, Marco is the ambitious one — the only one who sees the expedition as an opportunity rather than a punishment.
Personality
While everyone else was sent because they were undesirable, Marco connived his way onto the force because he thought he could rise faster in a chaotic theater than in the structured hierarchy of District 22. He is competent, disciplined, and hungry. He follows orders precisely, not out of loyalty, but because he is always watching for the next opening.
He keeps meticulous records, maintains his equipment, and runs his pack with efficiency that the other Pack Leaders lack. He is the one the Handler assigns for operations that require follow-through rather than brute force.
Flaw
Marco is too smart for his own good, and the other Pack Leaders know it. His ambition is visible. He is the one most likely to defect, sell information, or make a play for the Handler’s position if the opportunity presents itself. His loyalty is conditional on his own advancement, and everyone around him senses it.
In an expedition with no clear promotion path, Marco’s ambition has nowhere to go but sideways. He is competent enough to be useful and dangerous enough to watch carefully.
Tattoo Style: Active — Toggle
Marco uses toggle tattoos. He walks into a fight already prepared, his ink primed and sustaining. But he is not prepared for an ambush, because his style assumes he controls the engagement. He burns hot and pushes his limits, confident that his ambition will carry him through before his reserves give out.
He does not know when his time runs out. He will not stop to check.
His tuner is pushed constantly for new applications and modifications. Marco treats them more as a research partner than a service provider, always hunting for the next innovation that will give him an edge over the other Pack Leaders. His tuner may find this stimulating or exhausting depending on their temperament.
Status
Active. Operating in the Outer Backstreets of District 12.
Associated Encounters

None yet. First encounter pending.

characters/stray-dog-packleader-marcus.title: Stray Dog Packleader Marcus
characters/stray-dog-packleader-marcus.content:
Stray Dog Packleader Marcus
A Pack Leader in the Stray Dogs expeditionary force. Of the six Pack Leaders sent to District 12, Marcus is the quiet one — the unassuming variable that no one has fully accounted for.
Personality
Marcus is the one the Handler trusts, and that is the most revealing thing about him. He is dependable, unassuming, and quietly competent. He follows orders without complaint, maintains his pack without drama, and produces results without drawing attention. In a force of six Pack Leaders, he is the one who feels least like a liability.
He has no Italian heritage in an organization where Italian names signal belonging. He earned his place through competence rather than legacy, which makes him an outsider among outsiders. The other Pack Leaders do not quite know what to make of him, and he does not seem interested in helping them figure it out.
Flaw
Marcus has no loyalty to the Stray Dogs as an institution. He follows orders because he has nowhere else to go, not because he believes in the cause. If a better offer appeared, or if the expedition collapsed entirely, Marcus would walk away without a second thought.
His flaw is dispassion. He cares about nothing, and a man who cares about nothing cannot be relied upon when the mission requires sacrifice. The Handler trusts him to execute, but the Handler also knows that trust is conditional on Marcus’s own assessment of where his best interests lie.
Tattoo Style: Proactive
Marcus uses proactive tattoos. He studies the terrain, analyzes the opponent, and primes his charges before a fight begins. He spends them deliberately, conserving what he does not need and committing fully when the opening appears. His dispassion, which the Handler reads as a weakness, is precisely what makes his proactive style effective. A clear head does not make heat-of-battle mistakes.
His tuner has the quietest relationship of any in the expedition. Maintenance on a schedule. New applications only when tactically justified. Marcus does not experiment. He does not show off. He does not request upgrades for status. His ink is maintained well enough to function, distinctive enough to go unnoticed. Exactly the way he wants it.
Status
Active. Operating in the Outer Backstreets of District 12.
Associated Encounters

None yet. First encounter pending.

characters/stray-dog-packleader-rocco.title: Stray Dog Packleader Rocco
characters/stray-dog-packleader-rocco.content:
Stray Dog Packleader Rocco
A Pack Leader in the Stray Dogs expeditionary force. Of the six Pack Leaders sent to District 12, Rocco is the caretaker — the one who treats his pack as family rather than assets.
Personality
Over-reliant to a fault on his packmates. Friendly to a fault. Emotional, vengeful when one of his people is wronged. Rocco found the first real family he has ever had in the Stray Dogs, and he will burn the entire district down to protect it. He cares less about the Thumb’s objectives than about whether his people ate today.
He is the Pack Leader most likely to pick a fight he cannot win because someone he loves was hurt, and the most likely to shelter deserters from other Packs because he cannot turn away someone who needs help. His loyalty is genuine and fierce, which makes him both the most dependable and the most dangerous member of the expedition in equal measure.
Flaw
Rocco is too good for the organization he serves. In a different syndicate, he would be the most loyal captain they ever had. But the Stray Dogs are an expeditionary force of undesirables sent to die in a quarantine zone, and Rocco keeps trying to build a family in a place where families get used as leverage.
The Handler keeps him on a longer leash than the others because Rocco is the least likely to scheme. But that also makes him the most likely to do something catastrophic out of love.
Tattoo Style: Passive
Rocco uses passive tattoos exclusively. He does not care about the intricacies of ink mechanics, activation timing, or tactical loadouts. He wants a permanent upgrade that he never has to think about, so he can focus his attention where it matters: his pack. The tradeoffs of passive ink, slower movement, faster fatigue, reduced flexibility, he accepts them without complaint because thinking about them would take time away from his people.
His tattoos are applied by a tuner he trusts, the same one who has done all his work since District 22. Rocco prioritizes pack-wide maintenance. His tuner works on his people before him. When he requests new applications, they are always for the benefit of the group, not himself.
Counterpart
Rocco is the structural opposite of Bosco. Where Bosco could not hold his pack together because he did not want to, Rocco cannot hold his pack together because he cares too much. His emotional investment makes him predictable to enemies and frustrating to the Handler.
Status
Active. Operating in the Outer Backstreets of District 12.
Associated Encounters

None yet. First encounter pending.

characters/stray-dog-packleader-valentin.title: Stray Dog Packleader Valentina
characters/stray-dog-packleader-valentin.content:
Stray Dog Packleader Valentina
A Pack Leader in the Stray Dogs expeditionary force. Of the six Pack Leaders sent to District 12, Valentina is the sadist — the one who enjoys the hunt and the kill more than the hold.
Personality
Valentina takes territory efficiently but then terrorizes the local population. She burns goodwill, generates resistance, and makes the Thumb’s long-term occupation harder with every victory she claims. She does not care. For her, the expedition is not about territory or orders. It is about permission to do what she would be doing anyway.
She is lethal in combat, fearless, and utterly without restraint. Her pack operates in a state of controlled chaos that somehow produces results despite itself. She does not command through loyalty or fear. She commands through the simple fact that she is the most dangerous person in any room, and everyone knows it.
Flaw
Valentina cannot stop once she starts. The Handler keeps her on a short leash not because she is incompetent, but because left to her own devices she would turn the entire Outer Backstreets into a war zone that no one can profit from. She is effective precisely until the moment she overreaches, and that moment always comes eventually.
The Thumb wants territory secured, not conquered. Valentina does not understand the difference, and no one has found a way to explain it to her that sticks.
Tattoo Style: Active — Burst
Valentina uses burst tattoos. She does not plan fights. She explodes into them. Her style is instinctual, overwhelming force in the opening exchange, and if that does not end the fight, she keeps burning. Burst tattoos punish anyone who cannot match her opening speed, but they also burn through the user the fastest.
She burns through tuners just as fast. Her burst style is hard on the ink and hard on the person applying and maintaining it. She has requested replacements multiple times. Her current tuner is either new, desperate, or somehow matches her intensity. If commercial work happens under her pack, the threat was implicit.
Status

characters/stray-dog-packleader-vito.title: Stray Dog Packleader Vito
characters/stray-dog-packleader-vito.content:
Stray Dog Packleader Vito
A Pack Leader in the Stray Dogs expeditionary force. Of the six Pack Leaders sent to District 12, Vito is the indulgent one — the one who enjoys the perks of rank too much to risk losing them.
Personality
Vito requisitions more than his share of supplies, bullies other Packs into giving up ground, and lives as comfortably as the Outer Backstreets allow. He is effective in a fight when cornered, but he prefers to let others do the dying while he directs from safety. He runs his pack efficiently enough, but his primary concern is maintaining his own comfort.
His territory is well-supplied because he takes from everyone else. His pack is loyal out of fear and dependence, not respect. He understands this dynamic well enough to maintain it, but not well enough to see that it is eroding.
Flaw
Vito has grown soft and does not realize how close his people are to turning on him. Comfortable quarters, good food, the best equipment — he has let his edge dull in the ways that matter most. A Pack Leader who directs from safety is a Pack Leader who has not had to test himself recently, and the Inner Backstreets does not care how comfortable he once was.
His packmates resent him. The Handler keeps him because he delivers results on paper, but his position is less secure than he believes.
Tattoo Style: Reactive
Vito uses reactive tattoos, and that choice is itself a statement of his character. His ink handles defense automatically. He does not have to think about it. He has the luxury of not paying attention, of letting the tattoos do the work that he should have been maintaining himself. The same way he lets his packmates do the dying while he directs from safety.
His edge has dulled precisely because his reactive ink has been carrying him. If he ever faces an opponent who can bait his reactions and exploit the cooldown, Vito will discover that his tattoos cannot save him from a skill he let atrophy.
He demands his tuner prioritize him personally. New applications, premium maintenance, the best of everything. His pack gets the bare minimum. If the tuner does commercial work, Vito takes a cut. His tuner knows they are being used for profit and resents it.
Status
Active. Operating in the Outer Backstreets of District 12.

factions/death's-head.title: Death's Head
factions/death's-head.content:
Death’s Head
A biker gang syndicate that controls territory in the Backstreets of District 12 — the campaign’s primary location. They operate through intimidation, extortion, and force, controlling checkpoints, patrols, and warehouse districts. Their reach expanded significantly after the L Corp. collapse (the “fall of the Wing”).
Hierarchy
The Death’s Head operates with a military-like structure:

Leader — Unknown to the players. The overall leader has not been revealed.
Road Captains — Sector commanders who control the four quadrants of Death’s Head territory. Four known Road Captains:

Jodi (Southwest) — Killed by the Kurokumo Clan for failure to keep her territory in line. The Kurokumo Clan set an example following the death of Stray Dogs Packleader Bosco.
Velder (Northeast) — Dressed like a welder. Killed by Agent Es in his campaign against the Death’s Head. Part of a different campaign.
Unnamed (Northwest) — No details known.
Unnamed (Southeast) — No details known.


Sergeant-at-arms — Enforcers and lieutenants. Brick served as Sergeant-at-arms under Jodi.
Armored Bikers — Elite members, heavily armored, serving as the backbone of offensive and defensive operations.
Prospects — Low-ranking members and foot soldiers.

Territory
The Death’s Head controls the Backstreets of District 12, divided into four sectors:

Southwest — Controlled by Road Captain Jodi (deceased)
Northeast — Controlled by Road Captain Velder (deceased)
Northwest — Controlled by unnamed Road Captain

Key locations include:

The Pound — Prison/detention center (see below)

Patrols — Armed groups patrolling streets

Their territory is in direct conflict with the Community, a civilian settlement also in District 12.
The Pound
The Pound served a dual purpose:

Death’s Head detention center — A prison location to send troublemakers and criminals
Stray Dogs recruiting center — The Stray Dogs would look for new talents to possibly take into their ranks

This mixture created unease, and the Death’s Head reluctantly kept the Pound running under the Stray Dogs’ orders. The Stray Dogs used the Pound as a pipeline for recruiting, while the Death’s Head maintained it as a prison — an arrangement that bred resentment.
Members

factions/night-witches.title: Night Witches
factions/night-witches.content:
Night Witches
A Backstreets syndicate specializing in gravity-assisted rooftop assaults and psychological warfare. They do not use illegal flight — instead they glide from skyscrapers, striking from above using patience, coordination, and exhaustion tactics. Their methods derive from Smoke War night-bombing doctrine, adapted for urban verticality.
Internal Name: The Descent
Street Name: “Night Witches”
Territory: 1–3 dense blocks with connected rooftops, alley networks, fire escapes, and scaffolding. They do not expand beyond familiar terrain.
History
The Night Witches descend from a small Smoke War unit that specialized in night movement, rooftop traversal, silent harassment, and disorientation tactics. They were not decorated soldiers — they were the ones sent where visibility was low and survival was worse.
After the war, these veterans returned to the Backstreets with no recognition, no reintegration, and no structure. They carried only habits, trauma, and tactics. Rather than forming a syndicate, they taught. The second generation — kids from the block, scavengers, lookouts — learned how to move without being seen, how to use height instead of strength, how to disorient instead of overpower.
When a syndicate occupied their block, they did not fight head-on. For days, strange noises drifted from rooftops. Smoke appeared in windows. Figures were glimpsed briefly on upper floors. Then coordinated descent attacks struck from above, hit-and-run strikes followed, and ground teams finished weakened targets. The syndicate did not get defeated. They left. That was the birth of the faction.
Philosophy

“The ground belongs to those who fear falling. The sky belongs to no one. We belong to the moment between.”

They believe falling is a form of honesty — gravity cannot lie. This aligns with Project Moon themes of inevitability and suffering.
Core Doctrine:

We do not fly. We only accept descent.
The ground belongs to those who fear falling.
The sky belongs to no one.

Their founder may have once attempted true flight and been punished by the Head. This turned legal restriction into ideology.
Tactics
Movement
Members use gravity-assisted descent gear: silk or membrane cloaks, bone-frame wings, coffin-shaped glide rigs, hooked cables to redirect momentum. They never gain lift — they only convert height into motion.
Legal Status: Not flight. To the law, it is descent.
Weak Tool Philosophy
Their equipment looks outdated or unimpressive: rusted blades, simple polearms, nail-studded batons, paper lantern markers, cheap masks. They do not win duels — they win exhaustion wars.
Signature Tactic: Engine Cut — Silence
Before attacking, they create absolute quiet. Methods include sound-absorbing cloth, abnormality-derived dampening charms, ritual breathing discipline, and urban wind masking techniques.
Psychological Warfare
They destroy sleep, not armies. Targets receive nightly “visits.” Windows open slightly. Objects move. Chalk descent marks appear overhead. Someone always survives to tell the story.
Small Team Structure
Roof Team (Descent Unit)

Pilot — controls glide path, chooses escape route, never fights unless cornered
Bomber — drops irritants, throws noise devices, observes target reactions

Street Team (Execution Unit)

Mask Bearers — gas masks, heavy coats, rusted cleavers, pipes, hooks. Move only once confusion peaks.

Ace Crew: “The Last Descent”
An elite team whose perfectly timed bell signals and coordinated strikes mark inevitable defeat.

Lowwind (Pilot) — never lands where expected, uses building drafts, carries no primary weapon
Ash Saint (Bomber) — carries handmade ordinance in prayer-like bundles, bows before every drop
Old Nail (Street Lead) — massive rusted cleaver, slow, direct, only appears once targets are exhausted
Third Bell (Watcher) — rings small metal chimes at precise intervals to coordinate movement

Escalation Pattern
Encounters follow stages:

Presence — strange sounds, distant glides
Discomfort — smoke, lights failing, supplies ruined
Exhaustion — no uninterrupted sleep
Panic Movement — enemy relocates or flees
The Ambush — descent and street execution

The ambush feels inevitable rather than sudden.
Equipment
Low-Tech Disorientation Ordinance

Lime Dust Bombs — quicklime in clay jars, reacts with moisture, causes burning irritation and temporary blindness
Pepper-Smoke Bundles — ground peppers, ash, soot, alcohol accelerants
Resin Smoke — thick clinging smoke that marks targets for tracking
Glass Chime Drops — bags of scrap glass dropped onto pavement for sudden noise

Combat Feel
When players fight them:

Enemies appear from above, not ahead
Combat begins mid-ambush
Retreat is vertical, not horizontal
Lights going out equals danger spike

Boss Encounter: “The Third Bell Operation”
Core Mechanic: Exposure Meter
Instead of only tracking HP, track Exposure (or Panic). Represents heavy breathing, loss of coordination, visibility breakdown, mental strain.
Exposure increases when players: sprint or chase rooftop enemies, separate from allies, attack blindly into smoke, miss attacks due to obscured vision, take sudden damage from above, act before coordinating.
Exposure decreases when players: hold position, move together, use defensive or patient actions, wait and observe patterns, prepare instead of react.
Phase Structure
Phase 1 — Harassment Battlefield: Limited visibility, bells ring periodically, gliders pass overhead. Ace Crew raises Exposure, not damage.
Phase 2 — The Mistake: Old Nail enters combat once party Exposure reaches a threshold.
Phase 3 — Predator Mode: At high Exposure, players misjudge distances, initiative shifts unpredictably, street team gains bonus movement.
Bell Timing
Every few rounds: First Bell (movement pressure), Second Bell (smoke or blindness), Third Bell (coordinated strike). Rewards observation, not aggression.
Secret Win Condition
If players keep Exposure low long enough, the Ace Crew recognizes disciplined opponents and retreats. Victory is psychological endurance.
Relationships

The Outmarch — Veterans show trauma constantly. Night Witches see them as potential threats.
Neighborhood Watch — Watch sees them as another不稳定 element to monitor.
Contractors — Contractors avoid their territory when possible.
The Community — Local power structure. Night Witches protect their block independently.
Smoke War Veterans — Spiritual connection. The Night Witches learned from soldiers who came home.

Reputation

“Don’t stay out after dark. The Night Witches fly.”

Among Backstreets survivors:

“If you hear the bells three times… don’t run. Running is how they choose you.”

factions/stray-dogs.title: Stray Dogs
factions/stray-dogs.content:
Stray Dogs
A subsidiary Syndicate of The Thumb originating and dominating the Backstreets of District 22 (V Corp). A pack of violent, punk-aesthetic thugs who control territory through force and augmented bodies. Sent by The Thumb to expand into District 12 following the L Corp collapse.
The Stray Dogs operate begrudgingly in District 12. Territorial by nature and reluctant to expand, they are undertaking this expedition under orders from the Thumb rather than ambition.
Origin
The Stray Dogs originate from District 22, where The Thumb’s influence dominates. V Corp governs District 22 and borders the back side of L Corp’s former territory and District 12, making expansion geographically natural.
They were sent by The Thumb to take up and control territory in District 12 following the L Corp collapse — exploiting the power vacuum left behind. As a subsidiary, they answer to the Thumb in the same way the Kurokumo Clan does. These subsidiaries work alongside each other when ordered, but they are not allies. A common superior does not make them friends. Conflict between subsidiaries is tolerated so long as it does not interfere with the overall objective.
Expedition to District 12
The Thumb ordered an expeditionary force of approximately 300 members into District 12. Not so large as to leave District 22 vulnerable, but substantial enough to demonstrate commitment. The force was drawn not from the Stray Dogs’ finest, but from members who were useful enough to keep alive but problematic enough to remove from home territory. The expedition serves a dual purpose: securing a foothold in the fallen district, and shedding dead weight.
Reinforcements from District 22, if requested, would take one to two weeks to arrive. Communication with the home territory is infrequent, as the Stray Dogs would prefer to have nothing to do with the actual territory they are being forced to take.
Territory
The Stray Dogs operate in the Backstreets of District 12 — the campaign’s primary location. Their expeditionary force is concentrated in the Outer Backstreets, where the fog is least concentrated and resembles an overcast gray sky. They are invaders and expansionists, pressuring existing District 12 factions — most notably the Death’s Head, whose local leadership they killed and whose territory they encroached upon.
They split their force across the Outer Backstreets territory, working alongside other Thumb subsidiaries (such as the Kurokumo Clan). Each subsidiary operates independently, acting in a land-grab dynamic, asserting dominance over local syndicates and conscripting them into service. The subsidiaries do not particularly care if their “underling” syndicates fight each other, so long as it does not interfere with the overall objective.
Hierarchy
Pack Handler
The expedition is overseen by a single Pack Handler — the one who holds the leashes of the Pack Leaders. The Handler is an older, known member of the Stray Dogs who has fallen out of favor. Their ideals no longer align with the Stray Dogs of the present day, and they were strong-armed into this position. Competent and unpredictable, the Handler was sent precisely because they were capable enough to control the Pack Leaders but expendable enough to be risked on the expedition.
The Handler moves cautiously. The death of a Pack Leader is not something to react to hastily — it could be a mistake, or it could be an organized attack. By being slow to respond, the Handler avoids falling into a potential trap, but this caution comes at the cost of leaving isolated members without direction for extended periods.
Pack Leaders
Below the Handler are six Pack Leaders, each commanding a Pack of roughly 50 members. Pack Leaders earn their position through strength and combat ability rather than administrative skill. This leads to suboptimal decisions and management errors, as a capable fighter is not necessarily a capable commander.
Five of the six Pack Leaders are variants of the same problem: violent, difficult to manage, and sent to District 12 because the Stray Dogs wanted them gone. At least one, however, is mentally capable and administratively adept — a genuine asset who happens to be leading an expedition of undesirables.
Pack Leaders do not cross each other’s territory — territorial boundaries are strictly observed. They are more heavily augmented and experienced than common packmates, with better equipment and more intricate tattoos signifying rank.
Known Pack Leaders

Analyzes the fight, primes charges, spends deliberately. Treats combat as calculation.
Packmates
Common members. Rank-and-file thugs who follow their Pack Leader. They are the expedition’s ground force, augmented through tattoo ink and armed with improvised weapons. Most carry Standard-grade ink, maintained by the Pack’s tuner.
Bosco’s Orphaned Pack
With Bosco’s death and no formal chain of command to reclaim his people, approximately 50 members were left orphaned. Bosco had already split them into smaller, unofficial groups to manage his territory — he was a lone wolf who kept his pack at arm’s length.
Their fates have diverged:

20 feral — Roaming bands with no leadership. These are the most dangerous and unpredictable. They take what they need and move on, indistinguishable from the lawless threat the Outer Backstreets fears most.
15 integrated locally — Pragmatists who have disappeared into District 12, taking work with local syndicates or communities. Hardest to track because they actively do not want to be found.
10 reintegrated with other Packs — The most disciplined of Bosco’s people, who have submitted to new Pack Leaders. Requires initiative and the willingness to accept a new chain of command — not abundant qualities in this force.
5 dead — Killed in the chaos, executed by locals settling old scores, or lost to the fog. Their names will likely never be confirmed.

The Handler has not moved to reclaim them, watching instead to determine whether Bosco’s death was a mistake or an organized attack. In his wariness, the orphaned packmates remain cut off from the syndicate that sent them here.
Body Augmentation: Tattoos
The Stray Dogs’ primary weapon is their own bodies, enhanced through subdermal nanite ink. The technology was originally a Wing Singularity — a proprietary augmentation system owned by a single Wing. When that Wing collapsed and its patent expired, the tech flooded the open market. Every syndicate, workshop, and back-alley artist has been modifying and reproducing it ever since.
Essenai
The generic term for subdermal nanite ink is SNI (Subdermal Nanite Ink), but decades of verbal abbreviation have corrupted it into a word that most people treat as a brand name: Essenai. Many argue about whether Essenai is the best brand or just the most popular, unaware that it was never a brand at all. It is the industry standard, the “acetaminophen” to everyone else’s “Tylenol.”
In practice, “Essenai” refers to the baseline standard-grade ink that most syndicate operations use. Every expedition, including this one, carries Essenai as its primary stock.
Quality and Modification
Tattoo quality is not a strict tier system. It is a function of the brand (the raw ink), the modification (the tuning), and the artist (the application).

Subpar — Cheaply mass-produced ink where drawbacks have not been engineered out. Diluted or poorly replicated ink sold for cheap. Tradeoffs are severe. Some subpar inks are modified to imitate higher grades, running harder but prone to burning out faster.
Standard — Does what it says on the tin. Side effects are known and documented, though not always communicated to the customer. What a knowledgeable person buys after doing research. Standard generic Essenai falls here.
Prototype — Mostly untested, specialized or experimental ink. Expensive. Trying to eliminate the natural drawbacks of a design, but the price must be paid somewhere. Typically developed by workshops or talented independent tuners.

The brand is the hardware. The ink source, the manufacturer, the raw material. Quality is the modification done to it. An artist can take standard Essenai and make it perform like a prototype through skilled tuning. A cheap artist can ruin premium workshop ink through poor application.
Tattoo Categories
Tattoo ink falls into five broad categories based on how it activates and sustains its effects. Each category represents a philosophy of combat as much as a technical mechanism.
Passive — Always on. The tradeoff is built into the body. The user acknowledges the cost and lives with it, permanently. A packmate with passive reinforcement moves slower or tires faster, but is always armored. Cannot be turned off, so the user learns to carry the weight.
Active — Burst — The user primes the ink and the effect happens in a single short activation. Requires intent, focus, and stamina. The fastest way to develop instinctual use of tattoos, eventually making them feel like a natural extension of the body. Also the fastest way to burn out.
Active — Toggle — The user activates the ink, and it sustains its effect until manually deactivated or the user’s stamina runs out. Avoids the permanent tradeoff of passive tattoos but carries the risk of continuous stamina drain. The user must end the fight before they hit their limit.
Reactive — The ink responds to an external stimulus without conscious input. An impact causes it to harden. A threat causes it to flare. The advantage is speed. The disadvantage is it can be baited or overwhelmed. A clever opponent can trigger a reactive tattoo deliberately, leaving the user exposed during cooldown.
Proactive — The user anticipates a condition and primes the ink. The effect is stored until that condition is met. Requires foresight, analysis, and a clear head under pressure. Flexible but demanding. A veteran who knows the district can use proactive tattoos with devastating precision. A panicking user carries dead ink into a fight.
Tuners and Ink Artists
The Stray Dogs do not rely on external tattoo parlors alone. Each Pack has access to a dedicated tuner — an ink specialist who handles maintenance, modification, and new application. Tuners are not subordinates of the Pack Leader. They are assets loaned by the Pack Handler and managed by the Pack Leader for the duration of the expedition.
This arrangement serves a dual purpose. The Pack gets consistent ink support. The Handler gets eyes inside each Pack. A Pack Leader who mistreats their tuner is a Pack Leader whose behavior the Handler hears about through a channel they cannot control.
Tuners fall into two categories:

Exclusive tuners — Bound to the Stray Dogs by contract or loyalty. They develop the cultural style that makes a Stray Dog recognizable on sight. The specific patterns, the punk aesthetic, the way the ink catches the eye before the fight starts. These are the artists who give the syndicate its visual identity.
Contract tuners — Independent professionals working a job. No loyalty to the syndicate. They tune standard-issue ink, handle maintenance, process bulk orders. They could walk away at any time, and the Stray Dogs know it, which means the relationship must be managed rather than commanded.

Each Pack Leader uses their tuner differently based on their personality and priorities:

Rocco prioritizes pack-wide maintenance. His tuner works on his people before him. If commercial work happens, it is because Rocco asked them to support a local community.
Marco pushes his tuner for new applications and modifications. He treats them as a research partner, always looking for the next edge.
Vito demands his tuner prioritize him personally. His pack gets the bare minimum. Commercial work goes through Vito, who takes a cut.
Valentina burns through tuners. Her burst style is hard on ink and hard on the person applying it. Her current tuner is either new, desperate, or as intense as she is.
Marcus has the quietest relationship. Maintenance on a schedule. New applications only when tactically justified. His tuner has the most free time of any in the expedition.

Tattoo Parlor
The Stray Dogs operate a tattoo parlor on the seventh floor of a multi-story building (above Summit Accounting and Blue Rock Holdings, below a hair salon). The independent artist there works with Stray Dog ink but is not a member himself. He offers body augmentation services:

Full body double-pattern enhancement: 3,000,000 Ahn
Per limb pair (two-pattern): 750,000 Ahn
Single limb single-pattern: 250,000 Ahn (200,000 for regulars)
Credit available for those with insurance, Syndicate backing, or Fixer license
The artist noted the Stray Dogs are “bad for business” due to the trouble they attract

Equipment

Street clothing with punk aesthetic — ragged, torn, deliberately rough
Improvised weapons — pipes, bats, machetes, brass knuckles, and similar
Body augmentation tattoos — their primary combat enhancement
Accessories — items that augment or mimic tattoo powers

Faction Conflicts

Death’s Head — The Stray Dogs killed the local Death’s Head leadership (shotgun woman and her second-in-command) and have been expanding into their territory. Death’s Head members are fleeing.
The Community — Some residents are scared of heading out due to Stray Dog activity in the area.
Lavender/Agent Scoot — Has a grudge against the Stray Dogs and sought to recover relics from groups holding them.
Local Syndicates — The Stray Dogs conscript local operations into service. These underlings are permitted to fight among themselves so long as the overall objective is not compromised.
Kurokumo Clan — Fellow Thumb subsidiary. Not allies. A common superior, but the groups are not friends.
Night Witches — The Stray Dogs have encroached on Night Witches territory, with feral remnants of Bosco’s pack causing disappearances that the Night Witches are being blamed for.

Strengths

Territorial organization with clear pack structure
Body augmentation tattoos provide enhanced combat abilities
Accessories that mimic tattoo powers add versatility
Fierce loyalty and pack bonds
Willingness to use violence to expand territory
Dedicated tuners for ink maintenance and modification
Expeditionary force of ~300 with additional local conscripts

Weaknesses

Tattoos only work when activated — catching them off guard neutralizes their advantage
Pack Leaders are combat-promoted, not administratively capable — suboptimal decisions are common
Pack Handler moves cautiously, leading to slow response times and isolated members
The force was drawn from undesirables — loyalty and competence are inconsistent

items/equipment/armor,-''highway''-set-(.content:
Armor, “Highway” Set (Mechanic’s)
A lightweight improvised armor set recovered from the Mechanic’s Workshop bunker. Built around a long leather duster with thin metal plates sewn into the fabric, allowing the wearer to retain most of their mobility. Reinforced with rubber from thick tires at key points. The pants have tire rubber sewn in over the thighs and shins. A leather hood stored within the duster is reinforced with rubber and steel. Rows of deep pockets are sewn throughout the interior. The boots are rubberized and long, reinforced with metal at the toes. Intended to be worn over one’s clothes and optional protective vest.
Comprised of

Long leather duster (thin metal plates sewn in)
Tire rubber reinforcement (thighs, shins, key points)

items/equipment/armor,-''offroad''-set-(.content:
Armor, “Offroad” Set (Mechanic’s)
A heavy improvised armor set recovered from the Mechanic’s Workshop bunker. An amalgamation of leather and sheet metal built around a thick, heavy duster with layered metal plates forming a chestguard, groin protector, forearm and upper arm guards, and shin and thigh guards. The helmet is welded metal resembling a bucket, with an integrated welding mask. Heavy construction gloves have extra metal protection and sheet metal covering the knuckles and back of the hands. Long rubberized boots reinforced with metal at the toes. Extremely protective but cumbersome, heavily restricting range of motion and producing a shuffling, clinking sound with movement.

locations/backstreets-clinic.title: Backstreets Clinic
locations/backstreets-clinic.content:
Backstreets Clinic
A medical facility located in the backstreets, run by a German-accented doctor with round spectacles, a medical mask, and mismatched latex gloves. The building is long and flat with a red cross above the entrance. Inside, a reception desk sits beneath flickering fluorescent lights — a cage of white doves occupies the chair where a receptionist would normally sit. The doctor speaks to the doves in a foreign language to calm them.
Services
The clinic provides advanced medical treatment including heliapoeisis therapy and fibrous mechanite treatments. The doctor is willing to work within a patient’s budget, though costs scale with severity. Expedited treatment options exist but come at a premium.
A gestator — a mechanical healing implant — can be installed for severe cases. The procedure involves surgical implantation and requires a recovery period. Upon discharge, patients are given a pill to expel the mechanites before they overbreed.
Notable Events
Burr was treated here after sustaining full-body electrical burns from electrified spike strips during the Death’s Head siege of the mechanic’s workshop (Day 7). Pug negotiated a treatment cost of 250,000 Ahn, which covered surgery, a week of recovery, heliapoeisis and mechanite therapy, and the installation of the gestator implant. Pug was given a key to the hospital room to visit during recovery.
The doctor found Burr’s response to the combined treatments remarkable, noting that no one had ever agreed to trial both heliapoeisis and fibrous mechanites simultaneously.
Connections

Koller — The doctor is familiar with Koller through the underground network.
German Doctor — The doctor who operates the clinic.
Key, Clinic - Hospital Room — Key given to Pug for visiting Burr during recovery.

locations/death's-head-clinic.title: Death's Head Clinic
locations/death's-head-clinic.content:
Death’s Head Clinic
A small pharmacy and medical supply shop located deeper within Death’s Head territory. The area is sparse — civilians are emaciated, pale, with sunken eyes and gaunt cheeks, and they avoid strangers on sight. Death’s Head patrols pass through occasionally, some members not even wearing their leather vests.
Description
The clinic is a modest storefront. Inside, the shelves still hold some medication, though they could not be called full. Fluorescent lights flicker but stay on. A tired man works behind the counter.
Inventory & Services
The clinic once stocked Helapoeisis G9 (HP pills) — powerful healing medication — but most of its supply was requisitioned by the Death’s Head for their war effort. A small foil sheet of four 50mg pills was still available for purchase at 80,000 Ahn at the time of the agents’ visit.
The clerk is connected to the underground information network and is familiar with Koller.
Notable Events
The agents visited the clinic seeking HP pills (Day 4) but could not afford the cost. When they mentioned Koller’s name, the clerk’s demeanour shifted — he offered to deliver the HP pills himself in exchange for Koller’s location and left through a back door. Death’s Head members arrived shortly after, surrounding the building. The agents fled, pursued by an armored biker through the alley maze.
Connections

Koller — The clerk is familiar with Koller and eager to learn his location.

lore/strike-face.title: Strike-Face
lore/strike-face.content:
Strike-Face
Origin
Before the Corps perfected kinetic-energy manipulation, the technology began as a simple ceramic trauma plate manufactured by an early, defunct iteration of what was then K Corp — not to be confused with the present-day K Corp, which produces the Heliapoeisis healing drug and has no connection to kinetic-energy technology. The plates were stamped with a directional arrow and two words on the strike side: “STRIKE ← FACE” — telling the wearer which side took the bullet. Soldiers in the field began calling them “Strike-Face plates,” then simply “Strike-Faces.” The name outlasted the plate.
As Former K Corp refined its understanding of kinetic energy — absorption, redirection, dissipation — the technology miniaturized. The ceramic plate was no longer the vessel; the principle could be embedded into rings, chains, fabric, even tattoos. But the linguistic split was already complete.
The Split
At some point in the late corporate era, R&D formally divided the product line:























BranchDomainClean NameDegraded (Backstreets)StrikeOffensive — amplifying, directing, or delivering kinetic forceStrike Gear → StrikewearStrykewer → StrykeFaceDefensive — absorbing, dispersing, or nullifying incoming kinetic forceFace Gear → FacewearFaysewer → Fayse
The original plates became obsolete as a corporate product but never disappeared. They were too reliable to abandon.
Operational Tiers
Modern Strike-Face accessories fall into three functional categories per branch, regardless of form factor.
Fayses — Electrical Management
Defensive accessories themed around electrical circuit management: current, threshold, and load.
Fuse
Sacrificial. Single-impact. Destroyed on activation.
A Fuse detects incoming kinetic energy above a calibrated threshold, absorbs the full force, and shatters irreversibly. The wearer takes nothing. The accessory is gone.

Analogue: ceramic trauma plate
Cost: cheap, disposable, easily scavenged
Common forms: rings, thin chains, single-use plates

Breaker
Trips and resets. Absorbs a hit, goes dormant, repairable.
A Breaker thresholds similarly to a Fuse, but rather than destroying itself, it trips — dumping the energy and entering a cooldown state. It must be manually reset, repaired, or allowed to recharge before the next activation. While dormant, it offers no protection.

Analogue: steel plate — takes several rounds, then needs reworking
Cost: mid-tier, requires a Tuner or workshop for maintenance
Common forms: heavier chains, reinforced bracers, plate carriers with reset switches

Buffer
Always active. Dampens impact. Near-indestructible.
A Buffer does not wait for a threshold. It is a persistent kinetic dampener — absorptive material that bleeds force out of every impact. It lets damage through; it merely ensures the damage is never fatal in a single strike. Buffers are the most durable tier, and the most expensive.

Analogue: UHMWPE polymer plate — catches round after round, never shatters, eventually needs replacement
Cost: expensive, specialist
Common forms: suit-integrated linings, vest inserts, high-end bracers

Strykes — Thermal Management
Offensive accessories themed around industrial thermal control: heat buildup, venting, and dissipation. These are not fire — they are heat exchangers.
Flash
Unregulated thermal dump. Single-strike burnout.
A Flash converts stored kinetic potential into raw force with no thermal regulation — maximum amplification, all heat vented in one strike. Overheats the accessory, burns the user, and often destroys itself. The spectacle is the point.

Analogue: ceramic plate shattering on impact
Cost: cheap, dramatic, easy to scavenge but dangerous to use
Common forms: rings (Burr’s overheated bronze ring), single-use knuckles
Favored by: Stray Dogs — every punch is a statement

Flare
Thermal spike with cooldown cycle. Burst-fire.
A Flare delivers force in discrete thermal spikes, then cycles down to shed heat before the next activation. Hits hard, but the gap between bursts leaves the user vulnerable. More controlled than a Flash, still visibly aggressive.

Analogue: a temperature spike on a monitoring graph — sharp rise, sharp fall
Cost: mid-tier, requires venting period or external cooling between cycles
Common forms: heavier rings, gauntlet inserts, paired accessories for staggered cycling

Sink
Continuous heat dissipation. Always on. Never overheats.
A Sink converts kinetic force to thermal energy and disperses it steadily across its surface — no spikes, no venting, no burnout. It does not amplify as aggressively as a Flash or Flare, but it never hurts the user, never quits, and never needs cycling. A Fixer’s choice.

Analogue: heatsink — constant thermal load, constant dissipation
Cost: expensive, specialist, requires precision engineering
Common forms: suit-integrated panels, gauntlet plates, professional-grade rings
Favored by: Fixers — a working arm is worth more than a spectacular punch

Generational Layering






























TierWhat They WearWhoOriginalActual Strike-Face ceramic plates, legacy carriersWar veterans, old-timers, traditionalists. No fancy failure modes.StreetStrykes and Fayses in scavenged form factors — stolen rings, jury-rigged chainsScavengers, low-rank gang members. Whatever could be looted.ProfessionalPlate carriers with embedded Fayses; suit-integrated StrykesFixers, Syndicate enforcers, security contractors. The plate still catches the round when the tech fails.FactionSame tech, factional housingStray Dogs use chains and rings for visibility; Syndicate weaves it into tailored suits; zealots tattoo circuits directly into skin.
The plate carrier’s persistence at the professional tier is not nostalgia. It is pragmatism. When the kinetic layer fails — when the Fuse shatters or the Breaker trips — there is still dumb ceramic underneath. In The City, redundancy is not a luxury.
Vernacular
Modern Backstreets speech has long abandoned “Strike Gear” and “Face Gear”:

“He’s running double Fayses” — two defensive accessories stacked.
“That punch had a Stryke behind it” — offensive kinetic assist.
“Fayse popped” / “Fayse is down” — a Fuse or Breaker just triggered.
“Old man’s still wearing plates — swear to god, a Strykeface carrier from the war” — an antique, the technology in its original form factor.
“Needs a re-Fayse” — needs a replacement defensive accessory.
“He’s Flash-fried his arm” — overheated a Stryke and burned himself.
“Running hot” — a Flare mid-cycle, or a Sink approaching its thermal limit.
